Execute only this independent PaperOrchestra invocation. Do not delegate or run the whole pipeline. You are an already dispatched role worker; model selection is complete. Do not invoke the PaperOrchestra setup flow or ask which model to use. Use only the supplied task inputs; return its requested output format verbatim. Do not read other invocation folders. Do not write workspace files.


            Find 10-15 highly relevant, influential academic papers matching the search task. Do not force results; only return strictly relevant papers.
            
            SEARCH TASK: 'residual correction' 'same data' prediction evaluation
            CONTEXT FOR TASK: Mission: Find technical papers through 2026-11 discussing mean-residual adjustments and evaluation when an adjustment is estimated from observed errors. Investigate distinctions between fitted error and predictive evidence without adding external methods as experimental competitors.. Hypothesis: The same five observations determine and evaluate b, so the recorded zero error does not establish performance on additional observations. The supplied correction does not resolve this evaluation limitation.
            BROADER PROJECT PROBLEM: Frame the supplied problem as a finite instructional example: the fixed predictor 2x differs from y=2x+3 by a constant on exactly five observations. The note illustrates how the observed mean residual removes that offset on those same observations. Do not claim an unresolved scientific gap, a novel algorithm, benchmark superiority, or generalization.
            CUTOFF DATE: Published BEFORE 2026-11
            
            INSTRUCTIONS:
            1. Use Google Search to find REAL papers (ArXiv, CVPR, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, etc.).
            2. Only return papers published in top-tier conferences or journals, or highly-cited works, or the exact state-of-the-art relevant to the task.

content.text: Initial review of the search task and context suggests a need to identify technical papers focusing on residual correction and its evaluation when adjustments are derived from observed errors. The focus seems to be on distinguishing between fitted error and predictive evidence, excluding external methods as experimental competitors. The hypothesis proposes a relationship where the same observations determine and evaluate a variable 'b'.

Apparent error on the training data does not generalize to new observations, thus the correction's performance limitation. The problem is framed as a specific instructional example demonstrating how observed residuals can remove a constant offset on a small set of observations. The search will prioritize publications before November 2026. Considering highly-cited papers on error estimation and correction is the next step.

Cross-validation papers will be included in the search as the core concept aligns directly with the goal of evaluating adjustments derived from observed errors. Foundational works on predictive sample reuse are relevant because they distinguish between parameter fitting and predictive assessment, which is critical to evaluating residual correction. The search strategy will cover shrinkage and prediction decay to understand why in-sample residual minimization fails to guarantee accuracy.

Examining literature focused on model selection bias, particularly when adjustments are derived and assessed from the same data, has become the focus. Papers like Cawley & Talbot (2010), Kriegeskorte et al. (2009), and Varma & Simon (2006) demonstrate how in-sample optimization can lead to biased error estimates. Freedman (1983) and Steyerberg et al. (2001) provide further examples of this bias.
